title: Black Sea Grain Exports Face Total Shutdown as Russia-Ukraine Attacks Escalate
excerpt: Russia's grain lobby warns Ukrainian drone strikes could block all Black Sea export corridors, threatening food security across Africa and the Middle East as wheat prices surge.
body:
• Russia's Union of Grain Exporters and Producers warned that Ukrainian drone attacks could lead to a "complete blockage" of Black Sea grain export corridors.
  • Shipping through the Sea of Azov and Kerch Strait — which handled up to 25% of Russian grain exports — has been halted since July 10 due to drone strikes.
  • Ukraine has lost roughly one-third of its Black Sea port export capacity, dropping from 6 million to about 4 million metric tons per month.
  • Global wheat prices have climbed steadily as both sides escalate attacks on agricultural infrastructure during peak harvest season.

Russia Warns of Imminent Export Collapse

Russia's main grain lobby group warned on Friday that Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian ships and ports could shut down grain exports via the Black Sea entirely, pushing up prices and causing hunger in Africa and the Middle East.

The Union of Grain Exporters and Producers told Reuters that the consequences of what it called Ukraine's "systematic attacks" would soon be felt globally.

"The disruption to shipping in the Black Sea caused by Ukrainian attacks on dry cargo vessels and port infrastructure poses a direct threat to global food security."

— Russia's Union of Grain Exporters and Producers, in a statement to Reuters

The union warned that while importers have not yet faced outright grain shortages — thanks to carryover stocks and the temporary ability to source from other suppliers — "the consequences of this crisis will soon affect many countries."

Taman Terminal Struck, Azov Shipping Frozen

The warning came a day after a Ukrainian drone attack inflicted "significant damage" on a major grain export terminal at Russia's port of Taman on the Kerch Strait, according to an agricultural market source cited by Reuters. The terminal, controlled by Demetra — one of Russia's largest agricultural firms — has a capacity of 5 million metric tons. Demetra declined to comment.

In a separate Thursday attack, Ukrainian drones also struck a sunflower oil export facility at Taman owned by Efko, another major Russian agribusiness firm.

Shipping in the Sea of Azov and the Kerch Strait has been at a standstill since July 10 due to drone attacks. Those waterways previously handled up to one-quarter of all Russian grain exports. Russian exporters have attempted to reroute grain by truck and rail to deep-sea Black Sea terminals, but attacks on those ports have also intensified.

Ukraine's Ports Under Siege Too

The disruption is not one-sided. Ukraine's largest farming union, UAC, has warned in recent weeks that Russian missile and drone strikes on shipping near the southern port of Odesa are restricting Ukrainian exports during the critical harvest period.

Ukraine has lost about one-third of its capacity to export grain via its Black Sea ports, according to UAC. Under a deal meant to allow both countries to ship grain through the Black Sea, the Odesa-region ports had been handling about 6 million metric tons of cargo monthly. That figure has dropped to approximately 4 million tons.

"Russia has begun systematically striking port infrastructure, terminals and the entire transport logistics chain, using ballistic missiles again and again," UAC's trading department said in a weekly report, according to Reuters.

Ukraine accounts for about 6% of global wheat exports and roughly 11% of global corn exports, meaning prolonged disruptions could ripple through international markets.

Wheat Prices Climb as Both Sides Escalate

The mutual destruction of agricultural infrastructure has driven wheat prices steadily higher. Concerns over Black Sea supplies have added a significant geopolitical risk premium to grain markets, with fund positioning on the Euronext milling wheat contract reaching its most bullish level since June 2022, according to Fastmarkets.

The escalation in July has been dramatic. Ukraine's drone forces commander Robert Brovdi said the total number of vessels struck by Ukrainian forces in July alone reached 147, including oil tankers, dry cargo vessels, and tugboats across the Black Sea and Sea of Azov. Russia, meanwhile, has continued targeting military and industrial facilities in Kyiv as well as port infrastructure in Odesa and Pivdennyi.

The wheat stocks-to-use ratio among major exporters has fallen to roughly 18% — its lowest level in seven years — leaving little buffer against further supply shocks.

What to Watch

India, which resumed wheat exports earlier this year after a four-year ban with a quota of 2.5 million tons, could emerge as a partial alternative supplier if Black Sea disruptions persist. However, Indian wheat remains priced at a premium — roughly $20 per ton above Australian and Black Sea supplies — limiting its competitiveness for all but the most urgent buyers.

The critical question is whether the mutual escalation in the Black Sea can be contained or reversed. If attacks continue at their current pace, the Russian grain union's warning of a "complete blockage of export corridors" may prove prescient, with the heaviest consequences falling on food-importing nations in Africa and the Middle East that depend heavily on Black Sea wheat.
image_caption: The Port of Odesa, a key Black Sea grain export hub now facing potential shutdown amid escalating Russia-Ukraine attacks.
nri_angle: Rising global wheat prices and supply disruptions in the Black Sea region could affect food costs for Indian diaspora communities worldwide, while India's recent resumption of wheat exports positions it as an alternative supplier.
